title: Model routing
subtitle: How to build and measure routers that send simple work to cheap models and hard work to expensive ones — without assuming the router helps.

takeaways: Routing is a hypothesis: measure cost, latency, success and escalation together.
Confidence cascades can recover frontier-like accuracy at lower average cost — when evaluated carefully.
High-cardinality routing is a different problem than binary urgency.

body.text: Why this matters

A single premium reasoning model is operationally simple and economically brutal. Routing promises Pareto improvement. Many routers quietly destroy quality by under-sending hard tasks or thrashing between models.

body.text: Patterns

items: Decision-model router (Choice over tiers) — flexible, measurable.
Confidence cascade — try cheap, escalate if confidence low (AyAutomate discusses cascades recovering accuracy).
LangChain ModelRouterMiddleware-style binding for a run — see their public post.

body.text: What to measure

rows: How often did we climb tiers?

body.text: What the public evidence suggests

OpenRouter’s triage example shows near-tied accuracy across Jev and strong LLMs with large cost gaps on a small set. AyAutomate finds high-cardinality routing still favours a frontier baseline on accuracy, with cascades as a mitigation. TypeSafe’s own cardinality note says Jev supports up to 255 choices and may use multi-stage scoring beyond that — an architectural constraint to design for.

body.label: Do not assume
body.text: Never ship a router because a blog table looked good. Replicate on your labelled tasks.
TenthMatrix methodology (Benchmark B)

Our lab defines fixed-premium vs intelligent-routing arms on the same items, reporting success, cost, latency and escalation. Until a live measured TenthMatrix run is published, the dashboard marks methodology rows accordingly.

Conclusion
Routing is an optimisation problem under quality constraints. Decision models are strong candidates for the router — not automatic winners.
